blocks.why: Normal night at home — nothing on for four days, so just keep the clock where it lives.
Same again; a steady rhythm now is what pays for the early block starting the 8th.
Hold the routine rather than drifting late on days off.
Standby tomorrow doesn't start until 14:00 local, but bank a full night in case you're called out and run to 20:00 or beyond.
Off the evening standby and straight to bed — tomorrow you start walking the clock backwards.
An hour earlier to be properly awake and contactable for the 06:00 local standby window opening.
Lights out at 19:30 local — brutal, but a 05:40 report with 85 minutes of road means the alarm goes at 03:30.
Home by 14:00 local; an hour down now takes the edge off so you can face another 19:45 bedtime.
Second of three earlies — the 06:10 report buys you thirty extra minutes, take all of them in bed.
Tomorrow is a four-sector 11-hour day off an 05:40 report; go in with something in the tank.
Third early in a row — protect the full eight hours, this is the day that will hurt.
Long lie-in after three earlies; the 12:20 report tomorrow means you can finally pay back the debt.
Push bedtime an hour later to start rotating the clock towards tomorrow's midnight finish.
Twelve-hour day ending at 00:21 local — a bankable hour before you leave the house, not caffeine at the far end.
In the door around 01:45 local; sleep now but set an alarm — you cannot sleep all day and still get down again this evening.
The 'day off' is really a turnaround: bed at 18:30 local for an 02:45 alarm and an 05:05 report.
Up since 02:45 after a four-sector day — a short one now, then eat, then a proper night.
Full night with a late wake to load up for tomorrow's 12h55 finishing at 02:10 local.
Longest duty of the month, four sectors, last landing at 01:40 — get an hour in before report, you'll want it over BCN.
Home about 03:35 local; blackout the room and take seven hours, but be up by 11:00 so tonight still works.
Second sleep of the day — the 05:45 report on the 17th needs an 02:45 alarm and there is no other way to fund it.
Short duty but a wrecked night behind it, and another 05:45 tomorrow — top up before the evening.
Back-to-back earlies: 19:00 local bedtime for the four-sector Dublin day.
First real recovery night in a week — nine and a half hours before a duty that runs to 23:41.
Four sectors ending near midnight; an hour now covers the last leg back from ARN.
Through the door about 01:05 local — sleep, but cap it so you can get down again tonight for another 05:45.
Split sleep again: the only way to reach an 02:45 alarm after a near-midnight finish the night before.
Big night after a ten-hour early; from here the roster swings late for four days so let the wake-up drift.
Report 13:15, land 00:03 — nap before you go rather than fighting it on the CDG sector.
Home just before 02:00 local with a 15:25 report ahead — a full eight hours is available, take it.
Tonight's last sector departs CDG at 02:15 local, straight through the worst of the body clock — go in pre-loaded.
Door at about 04:30 local after an all-night finish; sleep the morning, blackout blind, phone off.
Get one normal night back before another duty that lands at 01:54.
Four sectors to a 02:24 off-duty, then 85 minutes of motorway — this hour is the one that gets you home safely.
Last night duty of the month done; sleep as long as it comes, four days off start now.
Reset to a normal night — one late-ish bedtime is fine, then start walking it back.
Half an hour earlier; the 30th is a 04:35 report and the clock won't move on its own.
Another hour earlier — deliberate pre-adaptation so the last early isn't done on an all-nighter.
Bed at 18:30 local for an 02:15 alarm — the earliest report of the month, and it needs the whole night in front of it.
Home mid-morning off an 02:15 start; sleep the debt off before doing anything that matters.

conflicts.statement: The roster prints local times only ('All times are LOCAL to the station shown') with no UTC column, so every instant above is my conversion: LHR and DUB at UTC+1 (BST/IST), ARN, BCN, FRA, CDG and FCO at UTC+2 (CEST). All block times cross-check against this, and reporting is STD minus 40 minutes throughout as no sector is long-haul.
options: Sanity-check two or three sectors against crew control's UTC feed before relying on these instants
Note that none of these dates are near the 25 October DST change, so no mid-duty clock shift applies

conflicts.statement: Standby runs to 14:00 local on the 7th and the very next duty reports at 05:40 local on the 8th, meaning you need to be asleep by roughly 19:30 that evening — about five hours after coming off standby, and hours before your body will accept sleep.
options: Treat this as the highest-risk night of the first week and get a 45-minute nap in immediately after standby releases
Ask crewing whether the standby can be released early if unused
Report it as a fatigue risk in advance rather than after the fact

conflicts.statement: Three consecutive early reports on 8, 9 and 10 September (05:40, 06:10, 05:40 local), each requiring a 03:30-04:00 alarm and 85-minute commute, with the third being a four-sector 11h01 duty. Sleep debt compounds across all three and peaks on the longest day.
options: Take the planned early-afternoon naps on the 8th and 9th; they are load-bearing, not optional
Ask about a hotel at base or near LHR for the nights of 7-9 September to recover the 85-minute commute each way
Flag cumulative fatigue to the operator before the 10th rather than during it

conflicts.statement: Duty on the 12th ends 00:21 local, and the next duty reports 05:05 local on the 14th. The single day off in between must absorb a full clock rotation, so sleep has to be split into a morning block and an evening block rather than one night.
options: Set an alarm for the morning sleep on the 13th; sleeping through will make the evening block impossible
No alcohol and no caffeine after midday on the 13th so the 18:30 bedtime is achievable
Ask crewing whether the 14th could be swapped to a later report

conflicts.statement: A 12h55 four-sector duty reporting at 13:15 local and going off duty at 02:10 local, with the final BCN-LHR sector airborne through 00:35-01:40 — squarely inside the 02:00-06:00 body-clock low, at the end of the longest duty of the month.
options: Take the pre-duty nap on the 15th and plan controlled rest and caffeine timing for the BCN turnaround
Agree a fatigue call threshold with the Captain before the third sector
Do not attempt the 85-minute drive home without a break if you feel impaired at 02:10

conflicts.statement: The 16th is printed as a day off, but it starts with you arriving home around 03:35 local and ends with a bedtime of 18:30 to make an 05:45 report on the 17th. It gives no usable rest day and no normal night at all.
options: Treat the 16th as a duty day for planning purposes — no commitments, no driving mid-afternoon
Ask crewing to move the 17th, which is only a 6h43 duty and the easiest of that block to reassign
If sleep on the 16th does not materialise, call fatigued before report rather than after

conflicts.statement: Identical shape again: duty on the 19th ends 23:41 local (home about 01:05), the 20th is the only day off, and the 21st reports at 05:05 local for a 10h42 four-sector day. One calendar day off, two split sleeps, no recovery.
options: Split sleep as planned and protect the 18:30 bedtime on the 20th
Raise the 19-20-21 pattern with the roster team as a repeat of the 15-16-17 pattern
Consider a hotel near base for the night of the 20th to save 170 minutes of commuting

conflicts.statement: Three finishes past midnight in four days — 00:33 local on the 23rd, 03:05 local on the 24th, and 02:24 local on the 26th — with the 23rd's duty departing CDG at 02:15 local and the commute home landing you at your door around 04:30.
options: Take both the main sleep and the pre-duty nap on the 23rd; going into that duty on one sleep is not enough
Arrange not to drive home after the 23rd's duty — taxi, or sleep at base before travelling
Ask whether the 23rd and 25th could be spread further apart

conflicts.statement: The 30th reports at 04:35 local, the earliest of the month, requiring a 02:15 alarm — and it follows four days off during which the body clock will have settled onto a normal domestic pattern. This is the classic case where almost no sleep is obtained the night before.
options: Deliberately walk bedtime back across 27-29 September as planned rather than resetting to normal hours
Book a hotel near LHR for the night of the 29th and recover 85 minutes of sleep
Plan the post-duty recovery nap on the 30th and do not drive anywhere else that afternoon
